reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors report a photothermal catalyst composed of NiO and Ru nanoparticles supported on TiO₂ P25. This catalyst has been applied to the photo-methanation reaction, achieving notable CH₄ productivity under 15 Suns light irradiation. Photothermal catalysis has been highlighted as a highly promising approach for the conversion of CO₂ into valuable products, based on the synergy between photocatalytic and thermocatalytic mechanisms. Irradiation with visible light excites electrons in the catalytic material, generating electron–hole pairs that can transfer energy to activate reactant molecules. Simultaneously, the temperature increases the kinetic energy of these molecules, promoting their adsorption and facilitating the breaking of chemical bonds. This dual action helps reduce activation energy, enhance the reaction rate, and improve selectivity toward desired products, as demonstrated in this work.
However, the proposed mechanism is not entirely convincing, and several fundamental issues should be addressed prior to publication.
The authors propose hydrogen spillover from the Ru surface to NiO, which acts as an "effective channel" for H. They suggest that the interface between Ru and Ni–O atoms is crucial for efficient photothermal methanation. While I fully agree that Ru is an efficient site for H-spillover, and NiO has previously been proposed as a good candidate for CO₂ activation, some inconsistencies raise concerns. For instance, in the proposed mechanism, the formation of a continuous interface between Ru and NiO is essential. However, there is a significant mismatch between the amounts of Ru and NiO loaded. While the optimal catalyst contains approximately 1 wt% Ru, the Ni content reaches nearly 40 wt%. This implies that, despite HRTEM images showing some NiO nanoparticles in contact with Ru, the majority of NiO is likely isolated from Ru. Therefore, only a small fraction of the NiO would participate in H· transfer from Ru.
Moreover, the synergistic effect of Ru and NiO in the present case do not surpass the production of other systems reported in the literature containing one or the other element, as the authors show in Table S3 (i.e. https://doi.org:10.1002/aenm.201601657; https://doi.org:10.1038/s41560-021-00867-w; https://doi.org:10.1002/adfm.202008244).
Alternatively, Figure 1C shows a non-negligible contribution from light to the overall mechanism, which remains approximately constant regardless of reaction temperature. In addition, photocurrent measurements, XPS peak shifts, PL quenching, and EIS results confirm efficient charge separation. It is well known that NiO is a p-type semiconductor, while TiO₂ is an n-type semiconductor. In this system, they form a heterojunction. Upon visible light irradiation, NiO can promote photo-induced charge transfer to TiO₂. Moreover, small Ru metal nanoparticles exhibit broad absorption in the visible and near-infrared range, potentially acting as antennas to harvest photons, in addition to facilitating H-spillover. Similar systems have been previously reported by Chaudret and Garcia (https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201803022).
Overall, a photo-induced charge separation mechanism between NiO/TiO₂, enhanced by the photosensitizing effect of Ru, could be occurring instead of—or in addition to—the thermal mechanism proposed. Confirmation or refutation of this hypothesis should be supported by experimental and theoretical evidence, especially considering the low proportion of interfacial Ru/Ni–O contact sites.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors investigate the role of hydrogen migration dynamics in modulating the kinetics and thermodynamics of photothermal CO2 methanation. To support their experimental findings the authors employ density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate reaction pathways and hydrogen spillover at the Ru0–NiO interface. The theoretical simulations provide a mechanistically sound explanation of the observed catalytic behavior, and their findings align with experimental results.
Notably, the identification of a spillover-induced shift in *COOH adsorption configuration from Ni–O to Ni–Ni is an important insight.
The comparison of energy barriers across Ru(001), NiO(100), and their interface strengthens the central claim regarding enhancement through hydrogen spillover.
The authors utilize the PBE functional in combination with a Hubbard U correction, with effective U values of 6.3 eV (O 2p), 4.2 eV (Ti 3d), and 4.6 eV (Ni 3d), and they appropriately include van der Waals interactions. The choice of PBE+U is well justified, especially given the large unit cells in combination with AIMD simulations, where a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost is unavoidable.
Overall, I consider the presented work as novel, original, highly significant and to be of good fit for Nature Communication.
Overall, I recommend the manuscript to be published in Nature Communications if my comments have been addressed.
Since my primary expertise is in theoretical simulations, my comments will focus solely on this aspect of the manuscript.
(1) My main concern is that it is not clear to the reader how the authors obtained the U values. Were they calculated (e.g., via first-principles approaches) or simply taken from the literature? More critically, how do these specific U values influence the simulation results? Even if the values were derived in a somewhat first-principles manner, this still could affect the results as these methods are known to be error prone. More details on how the U values have been obtained and a brief discussion with maybe a test calculation on if the U values affect their results would improve the quality of the manuscript. This can be down additionally to the computational details already mentioned in the SI.
(2) In Figure S12, some values related to the calculated vibrational frequencies appear to be missing (or maybe this is just in my copy of the file). Also, it would improve reproducibility if the authors could give more details on how they calculated these frequencies. I am guessing they also employed DFT with the same settings for all other calculations? If so how do U values alter this? This could be explained with either a clear justification for the U values used (see point 1) or just some simple test simulations.
(3) The authors calculate binding energies and electronic activation barriers along the reaction pathway, which provide useful qualitative insights. However, it would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation if the manuscript included at least a brief discussion on the limitations of analyzing binding energies and electronic barriers alone, rather than full free energy profiles that account for entropic and thermal effects.
I do not consider this a critical issue given the high complexity of such calculations and the fact that the experimental findings support the conclusions. Nonetheless, including a short discussion acknowledging these limitations would improve the overall quality and completeness of the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this work, Nie and collaborators present a photothermal catalyst, (NiO/Ru⁰)/TiO₂, designed to enhance CO₂ methanation by improving hydrogen migration dynamics. The catalyst achieves highly selective and complete conversion of CO₂ to CH₄ through efficient H₂ dissociation on Ru⁰ and subsequent hydrogen spillover to NiO. This alters reaction kinetics and improves catalytic performance. Although the results of this work may be of interest to the photo-thermal catalysis community, from my point of view, this study is merely incremental and far from providing a ground-breaking advancement in the field of photothermal catalysis. In fact, Santamaria and colleagues recently reported a similar system to the one presented here, that is, a RuNi/TiO2 catalyst for the photo-thermal methanation of CO2 (see "Continuous photothermal gas-phase CO2 hydrogenation over highly dispersed Ru-Ni on TiO2." Catalysis Today (2025): 115440). In addition to this, the methodology for the photo-thermo catalytic tests is not fully explained (for instance, authors did not provide any details on reaction time) and the relative contribution of light and heat on the reaction mechanism is poorly described.
For all these reasons, I cannot recommend the publication of this work in Nature Communications. Detailed comments to support this decision can be found below:
a) Authors wrote: “To assess the contributions of photons and thermions to the performance…”. Do the authors indeed refer to thermions (electrons emitted from a heated material) or phonons (vibrations) instead? Please provide an explanation for this statement.
b) What is the reaction time for experiments shown in Figure 1? Are those productivities calculated at a single point corresponding to 100 % conversion? Authors should provide data points at shorter reaction times to study the evolution of the product distribution with time. This is particularly important in closed batch reactors where consecutive reactions may happen.
c) Is there any effect of the composition of the catalyst on the product distribution? In other words, the selectivity towards CH4 is always 100 % irrespective of the catalyst?
d) The influence of the irradiation wavelength is poorly described. As per these experiments, UV light would have a minor effect, whereas IR would largely contribute to the catalytic activity. However, authors should clarify if these experiments were performed at constant irradiance, otherwise, the comparison is not fair. Upon introducing cut-off filters, the total number of photons is reduced, which inevitably reduces the catalytic activity. To draw correct conclusions, authors need to make sure that the number of photons under different irradiation wavelengths remains constant.
e) The relative contribution of thermal and non-thermal effects on the catalytic activity has not been discussed. Is the system dominated by thermal or non-thermal effects? Which is the larger contribution? Is the role of thermal and non-thermal effects influenced by reaction conditions (light intensity, irradiation wavelength, temperature). This is a work on photo-thermal catalysis and these questions need to be discussed.
f) The methodology to assess catalyst stability should be improved. Authors performed a stability test consisting of 5 consecutive catalytic cycles, each lasting 3 hours, until the system reaches 100 % conversion. To have a better insight into the stability of the catalyst, I suggest authors to avoid testing the catalyst until full conversion is achieved. Stability tests should be performed at low conversions (below 50 %, ideally 20-30 %) to ensure that the system is at kinetic conditions. In the kinetic regime, the reaction rate is primarily determined by the intrinsic activity of the catalyst and is not significantly affected by external factors (for instance mass transport limitations). When stability tests are performed under kinetic conditions, any decrease in reaction rate over time can be attributed to catalyst deactivation. Therefore, in this case it would be more insightful to perform a larger amount of cycles (10 or more) at shorter reaction times.
g) Authors claim that “Additionally, the H-spillover in NR-TiO2 was further corroborated using the WO3 color reaction, a well-established method for indicating the activation of H2 at the catalyst”. A reference should be included to demonstrate that this is indeed a well-established method.
h) In Figure S20, the images corresponding to W-TiO2 are missing.
i) In Figure 3, a), b), c) and e) letters are missing.

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors report a photothermal catalyst composed of NiO and Ru nanoparticles supported on TiO₂ P25. This catalyst has been applied to the photo-methanation reaction, achieving notable CH₄ productivity under 15 Suns light irradiation. Photothermal catalysis has been highlighted as a highly promising approach for the conversion of CO₂ into valuable products, based on the synergy between photocatalytic and thermocatalytic mechanisms. Irradiation with visible light excites electrons in the catalytic material, generating electron–hole pairs that can transfer energy to activate reactant molecules. Simultaneously, the temperature increases the kinetic energy of these molecules, promoting their adsorption and facilitating the breaking of chemical bonds. This dual action helps reduce activation energy, enhance the reaction rate, and improve selectivity toward desired products, as demonstrated in this work.
However, the proposed mechanism is not entirely convincing, and several fundamental issues should be addressed prior to publication.
The authors propose hydrogen spillover from the Ru surface to NiO, which acts as an "effective channel" for H. They suggest that the interface between Ru and Ni–O atoms is crucial for efficient photothermal methanation. While I fully agree that Ru is an efficient site for H-spillover, and NiO has previously been proposed as a good candidate for CO₂ activation, some inconsistencies raise concerns. For instance, in the proposed mechanism, the formation of a continuous interface between Ru and NiO is essential. However, there is a significant mismatch between the amounts of Ru and NiO loaded. While the optimal catalyst contains approximately 1 wt% Ru, the Ni content reaches nearly 40 wt%. This implies that, despite HRTEM images showing some NiO nanoparticles in contact with Ru, the majority of NiO is likely isolated from Ru. Therefore, only a small fraction of the NiO would participate in H· transfer from Ru.
Moreover, the synergistic effect of Ru and NiO in the present case do not surpass the production of other systems reported in the literature containing one or the other element, as the authors show in Table S3 (i.e. https://doi.org:10.1002/aenm.201601657; https://doi.org:10.1038/s41560-021-00867-w; https://doi.org:10.1002/adfm.202008244).
Alternatively, Figure 1C shows a non-negligible contribution from light to the overall mechanism, which remains approximately constant regardless of reaction temperature. In addition, photocurrent measurements, XPS peak shifts, PL quenching, and EIS results confirm efficient charge separation. It is well known that NiO is a p-type semiconductor, while TiO₂ is an n-type semiconductor. In this system, they form a heterojunction. Upon visible light irradiation, NiO can promote photo-induced charge transfer to TiO₂. Moreover, small Ru metal nanoparticles exhibit broad absorption in the visible and near-infrared range, potentially acting as antennas to harvest photons, in addition to facilitating H-spillover. Similar systems have been previously reported by Chaudret and Garcia (https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201803022).
Overall, a photo-induced charge separation mechanism between NiO/TiO₂, enhanced by the photosensitizing effect of Ru, could be occurring instead of—or in addition to—the thermal mechanism proposed. Confirmation or refutation of this hypothesis should be supported by experimental and theoretical evidence, especially considering the low proportion of interfacial Ru/Ni–O contact sites.

### Reviewer 2

The authors investigate the role of hydrogen migration dynamics in modulating the kinetics and thermodynamics of photothermal CO2 methanation. To support their experimental findings the authors employ density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate reaction pathways and hydrogen spillover at the Ru0–NiO interface. The theoretical simulations provide a mechanistically sound explanation of the observed catalytic behavior, and their findings align with experimental results.
Notably, the identification of a spillover-induced shift in *COOH adsorption configuration from Ni–O to Ni–Ni is an important insight.
The comparison of energy barriers across Ru(001), NiO(100), and their interface strengthens the central claim regarding enhancement through hydrogen spillover.
The authors utilize the PBE functional in combination with a Hubbard U correction, with effective U values of 6.3 eV (O 2p), 4.2 eV (Ti 3d), and 4.6 eV (Ni 3d), and they appropriately include van der Waals interactions. The choice of PBE+U is well justified, especially given the large unit cells in combination with AIMD simulations, where a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost is unavoidable.
Overall, I consider the presented work as novel, original, highly significant and to be of good fit for Nature Communication.
Overall, I recommend the manuscript to be published in Nature Communications if my comments have been addressed.
Since my primary expertise is in theoretical simulations, my comments will focus solely on this aspect of the manuscript.
(1) My main concern is that it is not clear to the reader how the authors obtained the U values. Were they calculated (e.g., via first-principles approaches) or simply taken from the literature? More critically, how do these specific U values influence the simulation results? Even if the values were derived in a somewhat first-principles manner, this still could affect the results as these methods are known to be error prone. More details on how the U values have been obtained and a brief discussion with maybe a test calculation on if the U values affect their results would improve the quality of the manuscript. This can be down additionally to the computational details already mentioned in the SI.
(2) In Figure S12, some values related to the calculated vibrational frequencies appear to be missing (or maybe this is just in my copy of the file). Also, it would improve reproducibility if the authors could give more details on how they calculated these frequencies. I am guessing they also employed DFT with the same settings for all other calculations? If so how do U values alter this? This could be explained with either a clear justification for the U values used (see point 1) or just some simple test simulations.
(3) The authors calculate binding energies and electronic activation barriers along the reaction pathway, which provide useful qualitative insights. However, it would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation if the manuscript included at least a brief discussion on the limitations of analyzing binding energies and electronic barriers alone, rather than full free energy profiles that account for entropic and thermal effects.
I do not consider this a critical issue given the high complexity of such calculations and the fact that the experimental findings support the conclusions. Nonetheless, including a short discussion acknowledging these limitations would improve the overall quality and completeness of the manuscript.

### Reviewer 3

In this work, Nie and collaborators present a photothermal catalyst, (NiO/Ru⁰)/TiO₂, designed to enhance CO₂ methanation by improving hydrogen migration dynamics. The catalyst achieves highly selective and complete conversion of CO₂ to CH₄ through efficient H₂ dissociation on Ru⁰ and subsequent hydrogen spillover to NiO. This alters reaction kinetics and improves catalytic performance. Although the results of this work may be of interest to the photo-thermal catalysis community, from my point of view, this study is merely incremental and far from providing a ground-breaking advancement in the field of photothermal catalysis. In fact, Santamaria and colleagues recently reported a similar system to the one presented here, that is, a RuNi/TiO2 catalyst for the photo-thermal methanation of CO2 (see "Continuous photothermal gas-phase CO2 hydrogenation over highly dispersed Ru-Ni on TiO2." Catalysis Today (2025): 115440). In addition to this, the methodology for the photo-thermo catalytic tests is not fully explained (for instance, authors did not provide any details on reaction time) and the relative contribution of light and heat on the reaction mechanism is poorly described.
For all these reasons, I cannot recommend the publication of this work in Nature Communications. Detailed comments to support this decision can be found below:
a) Authors wrote: “To assess the contributions of photons and thermions to the performance…”. Do the authors indeed refer to thermions (electrons emitted from a heated material) or phonons (vibrations) instead? Please provide an explanation for this statement.
b) What is the reaction time for experiments shown in Figure 1? Are those productivities calculated at a single point corresponding to 100 % conversion? Authors should provide data points at shorter reaction times to study the evolution of the product distribution with time. This is particularly important in closed batch reactors where consecutive reactions may happen.
c) Is there any effect of the composition of the catalyst on the product distribution? In other words, the selectivity towards CH4 is always 100 % irrespective of the catalyst?
d) The influence of the irradiation wavelength is poorly described. As per these experiments, UV light would have a minor effect, whereas IR would largely contribute to the catalytic activity. However, authors should clarify if these experiments were performed at constant irradiance, otherwise, the comparison is not fair. ## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors report a photothermal catalyst composed of NiO and Ru nanoparticles supported on TiO₂ P25. This catalyst has been applied to the photo-methanation reaction, achieving notable CH₄ productivity under 15 Suns light irradiation. Photothermal catalysis has been highlighted as a highly promising approach for the conversion of CO₂ into valuable products, based on the synergy between photocatalytic and thermocatalytic mechanisms. Irradiation with visible light excites electrons in the catalytic material, generating electron–hole pairs that can transfer energy to activate reactant molecules. Simultaneously, the temperature increases the kinetic energy of these molecules, promoting their adsorption and facilitating the breaking of chemical bonds. This dual action helps reduce activation energy, enhance the reaction rate, and improve selectivity toward desired products, as demonstrated in this work.
However, the proposed mechanism is not entirely convincing, and several fundamental issues should be addressed prior to publication.
The authors propose hydrogen spillover from the Ru surface to NiO, which acts as an "effective channel" for H. They suggest that the interface between Ru and Ni–O atoms is crucial for efficient photothermal methanation. While I fully agree that Ru is an efficient site for H-spillover, and NiO has previously been proposed as a good candidate for CO₂ activation, some inconsistencies raise concerns. For instance, in the proposed mechanism, the formation of a continuous interface between Ru and NiO is essential. However, there is a significant mismatch between the amounts of Ru and NiO loaded. While the optimal catalyst contains approximately 1 wt% Ru, the Ni content reaches nearly 40 wt%. This implies that, despite HRTEM images showing some NiO nanoparticles in contact with Ru, the majority of NiO is likely isolated from Ru. Therefore, only a small fraction of the NiO would participate in H· transfer from Ru.
Moreover, the synergistic effect of Ru and NiO in the present case do not surpass the production of other systems reported in the literature containing one or the other element, as the authors show in Table S3 (i.e. https://doi.org:10.1002/aenm.201601657; https://doi.org:10.1038/s41560-021-00867-w; https://doi.org:10.1002/adfm.202008244).
Alternatively, Figure 1C shows a non-negligible contribution from light to the overall mechanism, which remains approximately constant regardless of reaction temperature. In addition, photocurrent measurements, XPS peak shifts, PL quenching, and EIS results confirm efficient charge separation. It is well known that NiO is a p-type semiconductor, while TiO₂ is an n-type semiconductor. In this system, they form a heterojunction. Upon visible light irradiation, NiO can promote photo-induced charge transfer to TiO₂. Moreover, small Ru metal nanoparticles exhibit broad absorption in the visible and near-infrared range, potentially acting as antennas to harvest photons, in addition to facilitating H-spillover. Similar systems have been previously reported by Chaudret and Garcia (https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201803022).
Overall, a photo-induced charge separation mechanism between NiO/TiO₂, enhanced by the photosensitizing effect of Ru, could be occurring instead of—or in addition to—the thermal mechanism proposed. Confirmation or refutation of this hypothesis should be supported by experimental and theoretical evidence, especially considering the low proportion of interfacial Ru/Ni–O contact sites.

### Reviewer 2

The authors investigate the role of hydrogen migration dynamics in modulating the kinetics and thermodynamics of photothermal CO2 methanation. Overall, I recommend the manuscript to be published in Nature Communications if my comments have been addressed.
Since my primary expertise is in theoretical simulations, my comments will focus solely on this aspect of the manuscript.
(1) My main concern is that it is not clear to the reader how the authors obtained the U values. Were they calculated (e.g., via first-principles approaches) or simply taken from the literature? Even if the values were derived in a somewhat first-principles manner, this still could affect the results as these methods are known to be error prone. More details on how the U values have been obtained and a brief discussion with maybe a test calculation on if the U values affect their results would improve the quality of the manuscript. ### Reviewer 3

In this work, Nie and collaborators present a photothermal catalyst, (NiO/Ru⁰)/TiO₂, designed to enhance CO₂ methanation by improving hydrogen migration dynamics. The catalyst achieves highly selective and complete conversion of CO₂ to CH₄ through efficient H₂ dissociation on Ru⁰ and subsequent hydrogen spillover to NiO. This alters reaction kinetics and improves catalytic performance. Although the results of this work may be of interest to the photo-thermal catalysis community, from my point of view, this study is merely incremental and far from providing a ground-breaking advancement in the field of photothermal catalysis. In fact, Santamaria and colleagues recently reported a similar system to the one presented here, that is, a RuNi/TiO2 catalyst for the photo-thermal methanation of CO2 (see "Continuous photothermal gas-phase CO2 hydrogenation over highly dispersed Ru-Ni on TiO2." Catalysis Today (2025): 115440). In addition to this, the methodology for the photo-thermo catalytic tests is not fully explained (for instance, authors did not provide any details on reaction time) and the relative contribution of light and heat on the reaction mechanism is poorly described.
For all these reasons, I cannot recommend the publication of this work in Nature Communications. Detailed comments to support this decision can be found below:
a) Authors wrote: “To assess the contributions of photons and thermions to the performance…”. Do the authors indeed refer to thermions (electrons emitted from a heated material) or phonons (vibrations) instead? Please provide an explanation for this statement.
b) What is the reaction time for experiments shown in Figure 1? Are those productivities calculated at a single point corresponding to 100 % conversion? Authors should provide data points at shorter reaction times to study the evolution of the product distribution with time. This is particularly important in closed batch reactors where consecutive reactions may happen.
c) Is there any effect of the composition of the catalyst on the product distribution? In other words, the selectivity towards CH4 is always 100 % irrespective of the catalyst?
d) The influence of the irradiation wavelength is poorly described. As per these experiments, UV light would have a minor effect, whereas IR would largely contribute to the catalytic activity. However, authors should clarify if these experiments were performed at constant irradiance, otherwise, the comparison is not fair. Upon introducing cut-off filters, the total number of photons is reduced, which inevitably reduces the catalytic activity. To draw correct conclusions, authors need to make sure that the number of photons under different irradiation wavelengths remains constant.
e) The relative contribution of thermal and non-thermal effects on the catalytic activity has not been discussed. Is the system dominated by thermal or non-thermal effects? Which is the larger contribution? Is the role of thermal and non-thermal effects influenced by reaction conditions (light intensity, irradiation wavelength, temperature). This is a work on photo-thermal catalysis and these questions need to be discussed.
f) The methodology to assess catalyst stability should be improved. Authors performed a stability test consisting of 5 consecutive catalytic cycles, each lasting 3 hours, until the system reaches 100 % conversion. To have a better insight into the stability of the catalyst, I suggest authors to avoid testing the catalyst until full conversion is achieved. Stability tests should be performed at low conversions (below 50 %, ideally 20-30 %) to ensure that the system is at kinetic conditions. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors report a photothermal catalyst composed of NiO and Ru nanoparticles supported on TiO₂ P25. This catalyst has been applied to the photo-methanation reaction, achieving notable CH₄ productivity under 15 Suns light irradiation. Photothermal catalysis has been highlighted as a highly promising approach for the conversion of CO₂ into valuable products, based on the synergy between photocatalytic and thermocatalytic mechanisms. Irradiation with visible light excites electrons in the catalytic material, generating electron–hole pairs that can transfer energy to activate reactant molecules. Simultaneously, the temperature increases the kinetic energy of these molecules, promoting their adsorption and facilitating the breaking of chemical bonds. This dual action helps reduce activation energy, enhance the reaction rate, and improve selectivity toward desired products, as demonstrated in this work.
However, the proposed mechanism is not entirely convincing, and several fundamental issues should be addressed prior to publication.
The authors propose hydrogen spillover from the Ru surface to NiO, which acts as an "effective channel" for H. They suggest that the interface between Ru and Ni–O atoms is crucial for efficient photothermal methanation. While I fully agree that Ru is an efficient site for H-spillover, and NiO has previously been proposed as a good candidate for CO₂ activation, some inconsistencies raise concerns. For instance, in the proposed mechanism, the formation of a continuous interface between Ru and NiO is essential. However, there is a significant mismatch between the amounts of Ru and NiO loaded. While the optimal catalyst contains approximately 1 wt% Ru, the Ni content reaches nearly 40 wt%. This implies that, despite HRTEM images showing some NiO nanoparticles in contact with Ru, the majority of NiO is likely isolated from Ru. Therefore, only a small fraction of the NiO would participate in H· transfer from Ru.
Moreover, the synergistic effect of Ru and NiO in the present case do not surpass the production of other systems reported in the literature containing one or the other element, as the authors show in Table S3 (i.e. https://doi.org:10.1002/aenm.201601657; https://doi.org:10.1038/s41560-021-00867-w; https://doi.org:10.1002/adfm.202008244).
Alternatively, Figure 1C shows a non-negligible contribution from light to the overall mechanism, which remains approximately constant regardless of reaction temperature. In addition, photocurrent measurements, XPS peak shifts, PL quenching, and EIS results confirm efficient charge separation. It is well known that NiO is a p-type semiconductor, while TiO₂ is an n-type semiconductor. In this system, they form a heterojunction. Upon visible light irradiation, NiO can promote photo-induced charge transfer to TiO₂. Moreover, small Ru metal nanoparticles exhibit broad absorption in the visible and near-infrared range, potentially acting as antennas to harvest photons, in addition to facilitating H-spillover. Similar systems have been previously reported by Chaudret and Garcia (https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201803022).
Overall, a photo-induced charge separation mechanism between NiO/TiO₂, enhanced by the photosensitizing effect of Ru, could be occurring instead of—or in addition to—the thermal mechanism proposed. Confirmation or refutation of this hypothesis should be supported by experimental and theoretical evidence, especially considering the low proportion of interfacial Ru/Ni–O contact sites.

### Reviewer 2

The authors investigate the role of hydrogen migration dynamics in modulating the kinetics and thermodynamics of photothermal CO2 methanation. To support their experimental findings the authors employ density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate reaction pathways and hydrogen spillover at the Ru0–NiO interface. The theoretical simulations provide a mechanistically sound explanation of the observed catalytic behavior, and their findings align with experimental results.
Notably, the identification of a spillover-induced shift in *COOH adsorption configuration from Ni–O to Ni–Ni is an important insight.
The comparison of energy barriers across Ru(001), NiO(100), and their interface strengthens the central claim regarding enhancement through hydrogen spillover.
The authors utilize the PBE functional in combination with a Hubbard U correction, with effective U values of 6.3 eV (O 2p), 4.2 eV (Ti 3d), and 4.6 eV (Ni 3d), and they appropriately include van der Waals interactions. The choice of PBE+U is well justified, especially given the large unit cells in combination with AIMD simulations, where a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost is unavoidable.
Overall, I consider the presented work as novel, original, highly significant and to be of good fit for Nature Communication.
Overall, I recommend the manuscript to be published in Nature Communications if my comments have been addressed.
Since my primary expertise is in theoretical simulations, my comments will focus solely on this aspect of the manuscript.
(1) My main concern is that it is not clear to the reader how the authors obtained the U values. Were they calculated (e.g., via first-principles approaches) or simply taken from the literature? More critically, how do these specific U values influence the simulation results? Even if the values were derived in a somewhat first-principles manner, this still could affect the results as these methods are known to be error prone. More details on how the U values have been obtained and a brief discussion with maybe a test calculation on if the U values affect their results would improve the quality of the manuscript. This can be down additionally to the computational details already mentioned in the SI.
(2) In Figure S12, some values related to the calculated vibrational frequencies appear to be missing (or maybe this is just in my copy of the file). Also, it would improve reproducibility if the authors could give more details on how they calculated these frequencies. I am guessing they also employed DFT with the same settings for all other calculations? If so how do U values alter this? This could be explained with either a clear justification for the U values used (see point 1) or just some simple test simulations.
(3) The authors calculate binding energies and electronic activation barriers along the reaction pathway, which provide useful qualitative insights. However, it would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation if the manuscript included at least a brief discussion on the limitations of analyzing binding energies and electronic barriers alone, rather than full free energy profiles that account for entropic and thermal effects.
I do not consider this a critical issue given the high complexity of such calculations and the fact that the experimental findings support the conclusions. Nonetheless, including a short discussion acknowledging these limitations would improve the overall quality and completeness of the manuscript.

### Reviewer 3

In this work, Nie and collaborators present a photothermal catalyst, (NiO/Ru⁰)/TiO₂, designed to enhance CO₂ methanation by improving hydrogen migration dynamics. The catalyst achieves highly selective and complete conversion of CO₂ to CH₄ through efficient H₂ dissociation on Ru⁰ and subsequent hydrogen spillover to NiO. This alters reaction kinetics and improves catalytic performance. Although the results of this work may be of interest to the photo-thermal catalysis community, from my point of view, this study is merely incremental and far from providing a ground-breaking advancement in the field of photothermal catalysis. In fact, Santamaria and colleagues recently reported a similar system to the one presented here, that is, a RuNi/TiO2 catalyst for the photo-thermal methanation of CO2 (see "Continuous photothermal gas-phase CO2 hydrogenation over highly dispersed Ru-Ni on TiO2." In addition to this, the methodology for the photo-thermo catalytic tests is not fully explained (for instance, authors did not provide any details on reaction time) and the relative contribution of light and heat on the reaction mechanism is poorly described.
For all these reasons, I cannot recommend the publication of this work in Nature Communications. Detailed comments to support this decision can be found below:
a) Authors wrote: “To assess the contributions of photons and thermions to the performance…”. Do the authors indeed refer to thermions (electrons emitted from a heated material) or phonons (vibrations) instead? Please provide an explanation for this statement.
b) What is the reaction time for experiments shown in Figure 1? Are those productivities calculated at a single point corresponding to 100 % conversion? Authors should provide data points at shorter reaction times to study the evolution of the product distribution with time. This is particularly important in closed batch reactors where consecutive reactions may happen.
c) Is there any effect of the composition of the catalyst on the product distribution? In other words, the selectivity towards CH4 is always 100 % irrespective of the catalyst?
d) The influence of the irradiation wavelength is poorly described. As per these experiments, UV light would have a minor effect, whereas IR would largely contribute to the catalytic activity. However, authors should clarify if these experiments were performed at constant irradiance, otherwise, the comparison is not fair. Upon introducing cut-off filters, the total number of photons is reduced, which inevitably reduces the catalytic activity. To draw correct conclusions, authors need to make sure that the number of photons under different irradiation wavelengths remains constant.
e) The relative contribution of thermal and non-thermal effects on the catalytic activity has not been discussed. Is the system dominated by thermal or non-thermal effects? Which is the larger contribution? Is the role of thermal and non-thermal effects influenced by reaction conditions (light intensity, irradiation wavelength, temperature). This is a work on photo-thermal catalysis and these questions need to be discussed.
f) The methodology to assess catalyst stability should be improved. Authors performed a stability test consisting of 5 consecutive catalytic cycles, each lasting 3 hours, until the system reaches 100 % conversion. To have a better insight into the stability of the catalyst, I suggest authors to avoid testing the catalyst until full conversion is achieved. Stability tests should be performed at low conversions (below 50 %, ideally 20-30 %) to ensure that the system is at kinetic conditions. In the kinetic regime, the reaction rate is primarily determined by the intrinsic activity of the catalyst and is not significantly affected by external factors (for instance mass transport limitations). When stability tests are performed under kinetic conditions, any decrease in reaction rate over time can be attributed to catalyst deactivation. Therefore, in this case it would be more insightful to perform a larger amount of cycles (10 or more) at shorter reaction times.
g) Authors claim that “Additionally, the H-spillover in NR-TiO2 was further corroborated using the WO3 color reaction, a well-established method for indicating the activation of H2 at the catalyst”. A reference should be included to demonstrate that this is indeed a well-established method.
h) In Figure S20, the images corresponding to W-TiO2 are missing.
i) In Figure 3, a), b), c) and e) letters are missing.
